title: Requests for Startups, Summer 2025 — Full-stack AI Companies
author: Jared Friedman

dom.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

kp.k: AI-native legal providers could compete directly with law firms
kp.d: Jared Friedman proposes two business models conditional on believing LLMs can automate substantial legal work: selling agents to law firms or starting a law firm staffed with agents that competes with incumbents. He advocates the latter as a full-stack AI company. This is a proposed competitive strategy, not evidence of achieved legal automation, and the passage does not specify human supervision, professional rules, pricing or staffing ratios.
qs: Suppose you believe that LLMs are now able to automate a lot of legal work.
You could build an AI agent and sell it to law firms. That's what most people do.
Or, you could start your own law firm, staff it with AI agents, and compete with the existing law firms.

kp.k: Full-stack AI targets incumbent displacement across industries
kp.d: Friedman extends the legal example to any industry, especially those dominated by slow-moving incumbents. His recommendation shifts the startup's role from technology supplier to direct competitor delivering the incumbent's service; displacement is an entrepreneurial ambition rather than a documented market outcome.
qs: That, my friends, is going full-stack. You could do this for any industry, especially one dominated by slow-moving incumbents.
Instead of selling to the dinosaurs, you could make them extinct.

kp.k: Internal agents reportedly reduce term-sheet review and accounting time
kp.d: Pete Koomen reports that YC has built and uses an internal agent builder to reduce time spent reviewing term sheets and performing repetitive accounting workflows. He predicts every employee will build agents for repetitive work and identifies software access, permissions management and secure transmission of sensitive data as infrastructure requirements. The reported experience is not accompanied by quantified savings or output-quality measures.
qs: Soon, all companies will have one thing in common: every employee will build their own agents to automate the repetitive parts of their jobs.
It'll need to manage permissions, and send sensitive data securely to the latest generation of LLMs.
We've built a version of this at YC and we're already using it to reduce the time we spend on everything from reviewing term sheets to repetitive accounting workflows.

kp.k: Personal assistants would execute work rather than track tasks
kp.d: Tom Blomfield proposes assistants that understand correspondence, routines and preferences, draft responses, send messages with approval, schedule meetings and handle recurring processes without constant input. He frames this as performing tasks otherwise undertaken by a human personal assistant or chief of staff, rather than merely organising work. These are desired capabilities, not measured deployment results.
qs: Even the best organizational tools only help us keep track of what needs to get done—they don't actually do it.
Think of an assistant that knows how you typically respond to certain kinds of emails and can draft those responses for you—or even send them with your approval.
I want to see a system that truly does the tasks a human personal assistant or chief of staff might otherwise do, allowing you to focus on the work that matters most.

kp.k: Healthcare administration offers a large workflow-automation opportunity
kp.d: Gustaf Alströmer states that US healthcare accounts for over 17% of GDP or over 4 trillion dollars and reports estimates that one-third, or over 1 trillion, goes to administration. He attributes unnecessary administration to non-interoperable systems, missing APIs and manual data transfer. He describes startups emerging in the last two years to extract and organise data for agent-mediated entry into other systems, asserting substantial automation potential without providing outcome studies.
qs: The US healthcare system is over 17% of GDP or over 4 trillion dollars.
There are estimates that one-third of that, or over 1 trillion, is just spent on administrative tasks.

In the last two years, there is an entire set of new startups building infrastructure to extract data from PDF or other systems, organize it, and allow it to be easily entered with an agent into a different system.

kp.k: AI financial advice promises personalisation at near-zero cost
kp.d: Alströmer argues that existing routes to financial guidance are biased, lack a complete picture of users' circumstances or are expensive. He proposes API-connected LLM software supplying personalised finance, investment and tax advice at near-zero cost. Complete personalisation and unbiased advice are prospective claims, not demonstrated findings; the passage does not address professional oversight or regulatory requirements.
qs: They are filled with bias and don't have the full picture of your financial situation and goals.
And hiring a great financial advisor is very expensive.
With LLMs, there is a unique opportunity to build software that gives every person access to personalized finance, investment, and tax advice at near-zero cost.
They would use API's to access your complete financial situation and give completely personal unbiased advice.

kp.k: Voice models could transform business-customer telephone interactions
kp.d: Alströmer contrasts traditional phone systems and poor automated alternatives with new conversational models, claiming startups now produce voice bots indistinguishable from humans. He states that over a trillion calls exist between businesses and customers. This is an opportunity thesis supported by qualitative assertions rather than reported comparative testing or service-outcome data.
qs: But the new voice models and conversational LLMs are now incredibly good.
And startups who take advantage of them are are now making voice AI bots that are indistinguishable from humans.
Today, over a trillion calls exist between a business and a customer.

kp.k: Voice email tools could seed broader personal assistants
kp.d: Tyler Bosmeny proposes voice-based inbox triage, reply drafting and scheduling delegation. He presents email as a starting point for an all-purpose assistant because it contains personal relationships, plans and writing style, while his experience of arm nerve damage motivates reducing reliance on keyboards. These are proposed uses and personal motivations, not measured productivity or accessibility findings.
qs: I want to meet teams who can help me process my inbox – with just my voice.
It took me experiencing nerve damage in my arms to realize how much we still rely on keyboards for even the most basic tasks.
And email just might be the perfect starting place to build the most useful all-purpose assistant.
Anyone with access to my inbox instantly knows my friends, my plans, my writing style, and so much more.

kp.k: AI coding tools could shift designers toward founding companies
kp.d: Aaron Epstein predicts that easier product development over the next decade will increase the importance of design. Rather than treating AI solely as a job-replacement threat, he recommends designers use it to launch companies. He identifies empathy, problem-solving, quality standards and taste as founding capabilities and invokes Airbnb and Stripe as examples of design's importance, not as evidence of AI-driven occupational change.
qs: Over the next decade, as new coding tools make it easier than ever to build and ship products quickly, great design is going to matter even more.
Especially as many designers are worried about AI replacing their jobs, the real opportunity is for designers to use AI themselves to launch their own products and build their own companies.
The design job of the future will be "founder".

kp.k: Test-time compute could modernise scientific problem-solving
kp.d: Diana Hu argues that scientific software in chemistry, biology, materials science and operations research has changed little in decades. She identifies test-time compute as enabling startups to tackle scientific problems and recommends applications that make physical production faster and more efficient. No performance benchmarks or realised efficiency gains are supplied.
qs: A lot of the software tools used for scientific applications in chemistry, biology, materials science, or operations research haven't changed much in decades.
In particular, test-time compute is unlocking new types of startups that can solve these scientific problems.
We'd love to see more startups get created that use AI to transform how physical things are made faster and more efficiently.

kp.k: Reasoning and multimodality could enable individualised AI tutoring
kp.d: Harj Taggar contrasts mostly uniform online course content with a proposed personal tutor for every learner. He argues that reasoning capabilities support stepwise explanations and multimodal models support animations, 3D manipulation and voice. Grant Sanderson's educational videos illustrate the potential value of visual explanations, but the passage supplies no evidence of AI tutoring outcomes.
qs: Most online education products deliver the same content to everyone who signs up for a course.
And today, with AI, we think it's finally possible to build a truly personal tutor for everyone.
With the latest foundation models being multimodal, they can now present these concepts by generating animations, manipulating 3D objects, and explaining concepts with voice.

kp.k: Education transformation faces budget and purchasing-cycle constraints
kp.d: Blomfield states that education employs about 100 million people and educates about 1.5bn students annually. He anticipates AI improving access, personalisation and routine work, while describing study tools and grading platforms as early developments. He explicitly identifies tight budgets and slow purchasing cycles as business-model obstacles and predicts major change over 10 or 20 years rather than reporting established transformation.
qs: About 100 million people are employed in education today, and about 1.5bn students are being educated every year.
These technologies have the potential to significantly improve educational access, personalize instruction, and free both teachers and learners from drudgery.
One big challenge is figuring out the business model - while more than a billion people are engaged in education, budgets are notoriously tight, and purchasing cycles are horrendously slow.
If you fast-forward 10 or 20 years, it's impossible to believe that education is still going to be done in the same way it is today.

kp.k: Foundation models could expand robotics beyond controlled environments
kp.d: Hu attributes previous robotics limitations to expense, brittleness and dependence on controlled conditions. She claims foundation models now permit human-level perception and judgment and predicts an imminent breakthrough. She prioritises B2B industrial inspection and farming, citing Gecko Robotics and Bear Flag Robotics as examples, and recommends software infrastructure for robot builders. The capability claim is not supported by test results in the document.
qs: Robotics hasn't had its ChatGPT moment yet, but we think it's almost here.
But that proved elusive because previous generations of robots were expensive, brittle, and only worked in controlled conditions.
With the rapid improvements in foundation models, it's finally possible to make robots that have human-level perception and judgment.
We're interested in funding people building software tools to help others make robots.

kp.k: Commercial security capabilities motivate residential AI opportunities
kp.d: Bosmeny states that consumers spend $20B annually on home security and characterises major providers as legacy businesses with stagnant features. He describes commercial uses including facial-recognition entry, suspicious-behaviour detection and AI guards using loudspeakers, then proposes bringing AI-enabled security to homes. Ring's $1 billion acquisition serves as an opportunity comparison, not evidence of residential AI effectiveness.
qs: Consumers spend $20B year on home security.
Video cameras detect suspicious behavior and send push notifications to building managers.
Virtual AI guards will even come on loudspeakers and scare away criminals – to prevent crime before it happens.
Ring was acquired for $1 billion dollars for making video doorbells and magnetic door sensors.

kp.k: AI research ventures need not commercialise immediately
kp.d: Friedman argues that unsolved AI problems leave room for new independent research labs and supports deep, open-ended research taking years to commercialise rather than requiring a product within 3 months. He invokes YC's reported history with OpenAI as the rationale for this investment stance, not as proof that new labs will succeed.
qs: OpenAI is doing incredible work, but there are many unsolved problems in AI and still plenty of opportunity for new research labs.
Sometimes people think that to do YC you have to be able to ship a product in 3 months.
But actually, we're excited to back deep, open-ended research that may takes years to commercialize just like OpenAI did.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jared Friedman proposes AI-native legal-service delivery as an alternative to selling software to existing firms: founders could operate an agent-staffed law firm and compete directly with incumbents.
pts.d: In the principal section, Full-stack AI Companies, Friedman presents substantial automation of legal work as a supposition, not a demonstrated finding. He distinguishes a vendor selling an AI agent to law firms from a business delivering legal services itself. The latter is his full-stack model. His suggestion that entrants could make incumbents extinct is a conditional competitive thesis and exhortation, not a quantified displacement forecast. He extends the model to other industries, especially those dominated by slow-moving incumbents. The section does not specify legal tasks, the degree of human supervision, a staffing ratio, or whether all lawyers would be replaced. Elsewhere, Pete Koomen makes the document's other directly legal-work-related claim: YC already uses an internal agent builder to reduce time spent reviewing term sheets, alongside accounting workflows.

pts.k: The accompanying sections predict AI-enabled changes across design, customer service, science, administration, education, robotics, security, and personal advice.
pts.d: Aaron Epstein predicts easier software creation will increase the importance of design and create opportunities for designers to become founders. Gustaf Alströmer claims startups now produce voice bots indistinguishable from humans; that many healthcare administrative tasks can now be automated; and that LLM-based software could offer personalized financial, investment, and tax advice at near-zero cost. Diana Hu says test-time compute enables startups tackling scientific problems and claims foundation-model improvements make human-level robot perception and judgment possible, with industrial and farming applications especially promising. Tom Blomfield proposes assistants that execute correspondence, scheduling, and recurring processes rather than merely track tasks; he also predicts AI could personalize education, expand access, and reduce drudgery. Harj Taggar says reasoning and multimodal capabilities now make genuinely personalized tutoring possible. Tyler Bosmeny presents commercial AI security as a model for residential services and proposes voice-based email handling as a starting point for a broader assistant. Koomen predicts every employee will build agents to automate repetitive work. These are separately authored claims, not claims attributable collectively to Friedman.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The full-stack legal thesis is supported by a hypothetical example, while the wider document primarily offers founder experience, company analogies, capability assertions, and unsourced market estimates.
pts.d: Friedman provides no legal-task benchmarks, operating law-firm case studies, measured cost savings, or client outcomes for the full-stack proposal. His stated basis is an investment interest framed around a hypothetical belief in LLM capability. Koomen offers firsthand experience of YC's internal tool, but no measured time savings or quality results. Epstein invokes Airbnb and Stripe to illustrate the commercial importance of design, not to measure AI's effect on designers. Alströmer cites more than a trillion business-customer calls and estimates healthcare spending above $4 trillion, with over $1 trillion in administration; these establish asserted market scale rather than measured AI impact. Hu names Gecko Robotics and Bear Flag Robotics as examples of promising applications. Taggar uses Grant Sanderson's educational videos as an analogy for explanatory quality, not evidence of AI tutor learning outcomes. Blomfield cites approximately 100 million education workers and 1.5 billion students without sources. Bosmeny names Verkada and Lumana as commercial-security examples, gives a $20 billion residential-security market figure and Ring's $1 billion acquisition, and draws on his commute, nerve damage, and existing voice products to motivate email assistants. The scientific, robotics, and near-zero-cost financial-advice claims have no accompanying performance tests. In AI Research Labs, Friedman cites YC's relationship with OpenAI and research-investing experience to motivate funding research that may take years to commercialize.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The Summer 2025 document mixes claims of present capability with near-term opportunities and longer-term forecasts; the legal full-stack proposal has no dated displacement horizon.
pts.d: Friedman's legal example is conditional on believing LLMs can already automate substantial legal work. He gives no adoption schedule and discusses no jurisdictional, ownership, licensing, professional-responsibility, or verification requirements. Slow-moving incumbents are the explicitly favored competitive setting. Koomen contrasts present internal use with a universal employee-agent prediction described only as 'soon'; he specifies software access, permissions management, and secure handling of sensitive data as infrastructure requirements. Epstein's design forecast spans the next decade. Alströmer places healthcare infrastructure development in the preceding two years and attributes new automation possibilities to recent LLM advances. Hu describes robotics' breakthrough as almost here, with B2B applications immediately addressable. Taggar presents personalized tutoring as possible today. Blomfield calls educational AI early-stage and identifies tight budgets and slow purchasing as obstacles, while anticipating major change over 10–20 years. His personal assistant is a proposed product, including sending email with user approval, rather than evidence of unrestricted autonomous operation. Personalized financial advice depends on API access to a person's complete financial situation. Friedman explicitly allows research commercialization to take years.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The legal thesis concerns founders and incumbent providers; it does not make specific claims about legal clients, access to justice, or particular lawyer cohorts.
pts.d: Friedman positions founders as potential direct competitors to existing law firms rather than merely their technology suppliers. Incumbents face possible substitution by AI-native service businesses, but no firm size, practice area, jurisdiction, or client segment is identified. Although agent staffing implies a change in how work is produced, the document does not predict specific associate, partner, or paralegal headcount changes, billing-model changes, or effects on unmet civil legal need. Koomen describes employees, including YC personnel reviewing term sheets, as gaining time for less repetitive work. Across the accompanying sections, designers gain entrepreneurial opportunities; businesses and callers encounter automated voice interactions; scientific and industrial organizations gain proposed problem-solving and production efficiencies; healthcare systems gain administrative automation; students and teachers gain personalized tools and reduced routine work; industrial operators and farmers are early robot users; residents are prospective customers for AI security; email users, including those unable to rely comfortably on keyboards, gain voice interaction; and individuals gain proposed low-cost financial advice. Personal assistants and chiefs of staff supply the task-role comparison for Blomfield's assistant proposal, not a quantified employment-loss prediction.
